title: An Example of Deliberate Practice from my Actual Life
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart argues that the best way to teach character strengths is for teachers to grow those strengths themselves and show students, through their own stories, that the work is worth doing. He is careful to say this is not a new lesson plan: character instruction should not derail the curriculum. Instead, teachers should look for a moment in the week to share a real example from their own lives. He focuses on one narrow element of grit, deliberate practice, because breaking a skill into specific chunks matters when teaching any skill. His own example is three years and more than a thousand hours of learning the unglamorous craft of running a blog. He illustrates it with a WordPress video-alignment fix, the kind of task he never dreamed of doing but which served goals he cared about. He then adds a second half to the picture: in Duckworth's account, deliberate practice is fuelled by passion, and he describes the boring, repetitive work adding up to life-changing results. He closes with three walkaway steps for teachers to find, rehearse, and share their own stories.
points: Stuart argues that teacher modeling is essential, not optional, to character instruction: one of the best ways to help students develop character is to show with one's own life that the work is worth doing.
He deliberately narrows the focus to a single component of grit, deliberate practice, applying the general teaching principle of drilling down to specific chunks of a skill.
His blogging example is chosen to make deliberate practice look dull, repetitive, and slow to pay off, which he says is what it usually looks like in real life.
Drawing on Duckworth, he argues that repetitive practice is sustained by a long-term passion and goals the learner cares about, not by liking the individual tasks.
His three walkaway steps turn the idea into routine practice: pick a boring, slow-payoff example from your own life, rehearse telling it, and share it with at least one student that week.
quotes: And yet, this personal character growth is not truly selfish, either — not if our aim is to help our students leverage these strengths toward their long-term growth. Heck, it's not even optional because one of the best ways to help our students develop character in themselves is if we show them with our lives that this work is worth doing.

This doesn't mean coming up with a whole lesson plan — character strengths instruction should not derail curricula. Instead, just look for the opportunity in the week to share with your students an example of character strength work in your own life.

Externally, running a blog seems simple to many people I talk to. But over the past three years, I've put at least a thousand hours into figuring out blogging. That might sound like a lot, but it averages out to a little less than an hour a day.

So that's what deliberate practice is like in blogging: it seems complex on the outside, but mostly it's just very boring and repetitive. With every week, I pick up a few more tricks, a few more tweaks, a few more troubleshooting workarounds to problems I've not yet been able to solve.

And those things, my friends, are only possible through the use of deliberate practice. It matters not what your dream is: deliberate practice — boring, un-sexy, lame deliberate practice — is what dreams are made of.

I was driven by a desire to not just think about sharing interesting work and meeting interesting people, but to actually do those things. So I did (and do) the work, bit by bit, in the little snatches of time that I make, and the cumulative results of all those little bits of boring work over the past three years have been life-changing.
